nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: 8/17/92. T. D. Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory, Sarasota, FL.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: great barracuda
Scientific Name: Sphyraena barracuda

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthyes
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Sphyraenidae

Other Common Names:  barracuda (664 933)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No directed fishery, but caught by handlines, trolling, gillnets, and trammel nets (791 933). Marketed fresh or salted in Venezuela, Dominican Republic, and Mexico (791). Marketing prohibited in Cuba and some parts of Florida (791).

Recreational:  Reported by DeSylva (933) as an important recreational species, especially on charterboats on the east coast of Florida. Caught and mounted as trophies (933). Young up to 2 or 3 pounds regarded as wholesome in the Bahamas (871). The flesh of small fish is apparently not toxic although larger fish sometimes are (788). This species is responsible for more cases of ciguatera in Florida and the Caribbean than any other fish (932). There is no safe and reliable way of recognizing toxic fish (788).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role: A top predator which is known to sometimes attack man (788 932). DeSylva (933) provided a history of barracuda attacks on humans.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic, from Massachusetts to Brazil, and throughout the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean (327 788), and Bermuda (791). Found throughout the Bahamas (871). Occur only as stragglers from North Carolina northward (834). Also in the eastern Atlantic and western Indo-Pacific (791). Nearly worldwide in warm waters except the eastern Pacific and Mediterranean (327 788 933). Also recorded from South Africa and Kyushu, Japan (933).

Within Study Area: Present throughout Florida waters (791). Reported as very common in the Tampa Bay area (664). In the northern part of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), Snelson (997) reported barracuda as uncommon, but in the central part of the IRL, Gilmore (1009) found barracuda to be common. Juvenile barracuda often associate with seagrasses (1009).

Mobility and Migration:
Little movement has been shown through tagging studies on the west coast of Florida, but in the Florida Keys, one large individual was caught about 19 km from the release point (38 1042). DeSylva (933) suggested a northerly migration in the spring and a southerly migration in the fall along the Atlantic coast. He also reported that a similar migration may occur on the west coast of Florida (933). DeSylva (933) calculated a migration rate of 3.2 km (2 miles) per day for both the east and west coasts of Florida.

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs and young are pelagic (933 871).

Juveniles: Loose aggregations of juveniles often found associated with grass beds (933).

Adults: Larger adults are usually solitary in reef and offshore areas, and do not usually aggregate (791 933). Large schools have been observed, these are probably connected with spawning (87 1 79 1).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Eggs and larvae are pelagic in marine environments (871 933). Young are found in tidepools in the Bahamas, where they find both food and shelter, and they are also found in shallow grassbeds (933). Adults found in reef and offshore areas including the Gulf Stream (788 791 933). Also occur in deep channels (788 933).

Substrate: Young are often associated with inshore grassbeds and are also found over sandy bottoms (438 788 791 933 Gilmore 1989). Young also find food and shelter in floating Sargassum (933 1041). Adults found over turtle grass beds, in mangrove habitats, and over sand bottoms near fringing reefs and in deep channels (788 791 933). Common around oil platforms, wrecks, and reefs (327).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: No data on eggs available, but spawning appears to occur at temperatures from 22.8 to about 28.8 C (933). Larvae collected over a temperature range from 23.6 to 27.05 C (933).

Juvenile/adults: Juveniles have been shown to sometimes avoid temperatures of 34.1 C, but have also been collected in temperatures from 34.4 to 35.0 C (933). Adults will tolerate temperatures as low as 23.3 C (933), but have been collected at temperatures as low as 18 C (887). Barracuda in north Florida generally avoid temperatures above 28.3 C, but apparently are found in higher temperatures in south Florida (933). DeSylva (933) reported that they become sluggish at 30 C, but specimens have been collected on the Florida east coast at temperatures as high as 36 C (887). Barracuda are occasionally killed during freezes (236).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: Larvae have been reported at salinities ranging from 34.98 to 36.08% (933).

Juvenile/adults: Juveniles usually found in high salinity marine waters (438), but have been reported from 16.7% (933) and in the St. Johns River, Florida in salinities as low as 14.5% (885). Adults: are normally marine, occurring in salinities from 24.0 to 36.6% (933). Adults have been taken in salinities as low as 4.5% on the Florida east coast (887), and as high as 46% in Puerto Rico (934). Reported in freshwater in North River in south Florida (1043).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Fertilization is external, and both eggs and larvae are pelagic. Oviparous.

Mating/Spawning: Males mature at age II at a length of about 460 mm, and females mature at age III to IV at a length of about 600 mm FL (933). Spawning reported to occur from April through October in Florida with a peak in July (871 933). Secondary peaks may occur in May and September (933). Small juveniles have been taken in September in North Carolina (936). In east African waters, spawning apparently occurs from September through May (933 1044). Spawning probably occurs over deep water (933). Spawning is reported to begin when water temperatures reach 22.8-23.3 C and ceases when temperatures fall from 28.8 to 25 C (933).

Fecundity: In Florida, one female 895 mm FL contained 560,000 ova, and a female 1011 mm FL had 670,000 ova (933).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: Unfertilized ripe eggs range from 0.74 to 0.8 1 mm in diameter (933). Larvae, which are pelagic (87 l), range up to 11.9 mm SL (438).

Juveniles/Adults: Juveniles that were less than 40 mm SL in April reached more than 120 mm SL by December (933). DeSylva (933) gave the following mean lengths at age based upon scale annuli: Age I -less then 400 mm FL, Age II - greater than 500 mm, Age III - about 600 mm, Age IV - about 700 mm, Age V - between 700 and 800 mm, Age VI - less than 800 mm, Age VII - more than 800 mm, Age VIII - about 900 mm. DeSylva (933) also presented equations for length-weight relationships. Tagging data from Florida's west coast suggested an average growth rate for large juveniles and small adults of 5.6 mm SL per month (38). Randall (932) reported a maximum size of 1651 mm and 46.7 kg, but Robins et a1 (788), give a maximum size of 2 m and 48 kg. Reports of larger individuals are "unverified" (788). Said to live to an age of 14 years (871).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Generally daytime feeders relying on sight to obtain their food (933). The diet at all sizes is reported to consist mainly of fish (87 1 933). Diet of the young has been reported to be primarily fish, with clupeids, atherinids, cyprinodonts and gobies being the most important food items (933 Schmidt 1989). Other small, inshore fishes form a main portion of the diet in the Bahamas (933). Fishes associated with coral reef habitats made up 93.3% of the diet of barracudas collected in Florida by DeSylva (933). In eastern Africa, fishes were also found to be the most important component of the diet (1044). Squid are also part of the diet in the Tortugas region of Florida (837).

Adults have been taken in salinities as low as 4.5% on the Florida east coast (887), and as high as 46% in Puerto Rico (934). Reported in freshwater in North River in south Florida (1043).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Fertilization is external, and both eggs and larvae are pelagic. Oviparous.

Mating/Spawning: Males mature at age II at a length of about 460 mm, and females mature at age III to IV at a length of about 600 mm FL (933). Spawning reported to occur from April through October in Florida with a peak in July (871 933). Secondary peaks may occur in May and September (933). Small juveniles have been taken in September in North Carolina (936). In east African waters, spawning apparently occurs from September through May (933 1044). Spawning probably occurs over deep water (933). Spawning is reported to begin when water temperatures reach 22.8-23.3 C and ceases when temperatures fall from 28.8 to 25 C (933).

Fecundity: In Florida, one female 895 mm FL contained 560,000 ova, and a female 1011 mm FL had 670,000 ova (933).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae: Unfertilized ripe eggs range from 0.74 to 0.8 1 mm in diameter (933). Larvae, which are pelagic (87 l), range up to 11.9 mm SL (438).

Juveniles/Adults: Juveniles that were less than 40 mm SL in April reached more than 120 mm SL by December (933). DeSylva (933) gave the following mean lengths at age based upon scale annuli: Age I -less then 400 mm FL, Age II - greater than 500 mm, Age III - about 600 mm, Age IV - about 700 mm, Age V - between 700 and 800 mm, Age VI - less than 800 mm, Age VII - more than 800 mm, Age VIII - about 900 mm. DeSylva (933) also presented equations for length-weight relationships. Tagging data from Florida's west coast suggested an average growth rate for large juveniles and small adults of 5.6 mm SL per month (38). Randall (932) reported a maximum size of 1651 mm and 46.7 kg, but Robins et a1 (788), give a maximum size of 2 m and 48 kg. Reports of larger individuals are "unverified" (788). Said to live to an age of 14 years (871).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Generally daytime feeders relying on sight to obtain their food (933). The diet at all sizes is reported to consist mainly of fish (87 1 933). Diet of the young has been reported to be primarily fish, with clupeids, atherinids, cyprinodonts and gobies being the most important food items (933 Schmidt 1989). Other small, inshore fishes form a main portion of the diet in the Bahamas (933). Fishes associated with coral reef habitats made up 93.3% of the diet of barracudas collected in Florida by DeSylva (933). In eastern Africa, fishes were also found to be the most important component of the diet (1044). Squid are also part of the diet in the Tortugas region of Florida (837).
